PSYCHOANALYTIC PROCESS, PSYCHOANALYSIS ON DEMAND, CONTINUITY, CHILD ANALYSIS

In his book The Piggle, Winnicott describes a psychoanalytic process that began when his young patient was 2½ years old. He saw her for 15 sessions over a period of about 2½ years and he called this type of setting ‘psychoanalysis on demand’. He concluded that a child should either have analysis as daily sessions or be seen on demand. For an analysis ‘on demand’, the young patient needs a high capacity for continuity and linking to bridge the long intervals between sessions. The author examines in relation to the material of Winnicott's creative case presentation how this capacity was communicated to Winnicott by the small child (a kind of primary symbolization) and how these mostly preverbal communications were ‘heard’ (or not) by Winnicott.

A Psychodynamic Perspective on a Systematic Review of Online Psychotherapy for Adults

Diogo Machado , Pricilla Laskoski , Charlie Severo , Ana Bassols , Ana Sfoggia , Clarice Kowacs , Daniela Krieger , Mariana Torres , Marina Gastaud , Rafael Wellausen , Stefania Teche and Cláudio Eizirik

Cláudio Eizirik

[db_machado@yahoo.com]

Cláudio Eizirik   Psychiatrist and psychoanalyst, PhD in Medical Sciences: Psychiatry, Professor of Psychiatry, UFRGS, SPPA, Porto Alegre, RS, Brazil.
ONLINE PSYCHOTHERAPY, ADULT MENTAL HEALTH, ADULT PSYCHOTHERAPY, CULTURE, PSYCHOTHERAPY RESEARCH

A variety of new psychotherapy modalities has arisen in which the contact between patient and therapist takes place via the internet. The main objective of this systematic review is to investigate the types of online psychotherapy (OP) conducted nowadays, and to describe their main characteristics to psychodynamic psychotherapists who may wish to better understand the current scientific literature on the subject. The review used two databases, EMBASE and PsycINFO. Fifty-nine studies were retrieved and the main online psychotherapy modalities identified were self-therapy programmes using contact via email or chat; videoconference; and therapy exclusively via chat or email. The result of these studies suggests that OP is more effective than a waiting list control group. When compared with face-to-face therapies, OP showed similar effects. Most studies involved cognitive behavioural therapy; only two studies involved a form of psychodynamic psychotherapy. Different forms of communication allow patient and therapist to establish different relationships and therapeutic possibilities. OPs may be feasible treatment alternatives; however, it remains unclear, especially in relation to psychodynamic treatments, if therapeutic technique in OP, which involves changes in comparison with face-to-face therapies, would be useful in severe cases. Psychodynamic psychotherapists should adopt a posture of constant reflection on the changes taking place in the world and their impact on the minds of individuals, without, nevertheless, idealizing the ‘new’.

Rozsika Parker Prize 2016

Rozsika Parker, author of Torn in Two: The Experience of Maternal Ambivalence and The Subversive Stitch: Embroidery and the Making of the Feminine, represented WPF/FPC on the BJP's Board for many years. She remained a member of the Journal's Editorial Advisory Panel until her death in 2010. She was well known for her commitment to creativity, in both art and clinical practice, and our annual Prize, established in 2013, focuses on a critical engagement with this theme. The Journal is particularly interested in factors that support creativity in clinical or theoretical work, and those that may militate against it. In addition to the focus on creativity, the application of psychoanalytic theory to questions of gender; the arts; and social and cultural themes is welcomed. Authors should consult the BJP's submission guidelines (particularly in relation to confidentiality, where clinical material is concerned) and prepare their work with the Journal's Aims and Scope statement in mind. Advice will be available for questions concerning confidentiality, or eligibility to submit work.

The Prize has two entry routes: a Student Path and a Post-Qualification Path. Students or qualified clinicians are invited to submit original (ie unpublished) papers on adult, child, couple, or group psychotherapy or psychoanalysis, on clinical, theoretical, applied or research topics. The Student path is open to students on an initial clinical training, who are either currently in training or who have qualified within the last 12 months; and to students on university courses in psychoanalytic studies, and on university courses where psychoanalysis is a significant component. A student paper may have been submitted as part of a course requirement, if this is acceptable to the student's course, but the paper should be revised as need be to meet the criteria of this Prize. The Post-Qualification path is open to clinically qualified individuals only. Papers should be singly authored, but due acknowledgement should be made if the work is based on a joint project.

Brian Martindale

Brian Martindale

bm@bmakm.plus.com

Brian Martindale  

On initially opening this book, I was hit by two striking features. The first was that, not only does the extent of the New Library of Psychoanalysis series, the Teaching Series and the ‘Beyond the Couch’ now run into a fifth page, but the titles reveal the extraordinary contributions to contemporary psychoanalysis of this series. The second impressive feature was to read of Rosine Perelberg's own professional journey and her serious national and international collaboration over years within the British Psychoanalytic Society, University College and Birkbeck College, London, and with colleagues in Germany, France and the USA. I felt I was in for a treat in reading and reviewing one of the latest books in the series.

Perelberg's introductory chapter further whetted my appetite. She concisely introduces and summarizes the themes that she will ‘unpack’ in the chapters that follow. I anticipate that, like myself, there are many clinicians who have yet to grasp fully what is meant by the ‘dead’ father, its importance and distinction from the murdered father, or who could readily spell out the manifold oedipal constellations in the various psychopathologies they encounter, let alone the many different ways ‘thirdness’ is understood. The introduction also made me look forward to her bringing together the ideas of psychoanalysts and anthropologists in thinking about the incest taboo and gender differences.

In Freud's Totem and Taboo, the father who had access to all the women and ruled by terror is murdered by the ‘horde of brothers’ wanting the women for themselves. The law of prohibition of incest then becomes necessary for society to survive to prevent further destruction (through murder in order to have exclusive access) and this law is the unconscious nucleus of all religions (and civilizations). The dead father is here constituted as the symbolic father, more powerful than when alive, possessor of the phallus and representative of the ego ideal and the law. Sexuality is sacrificed. There is a fundamental shift from a narcissistic universe to the institution of the paternal function with the rule of law (culture). The chapter ‘Murdered father, dead father’ is outstanding for its illustrative clinical material of these themes from two men in analysis.

KIDS COMPANY, CHARISMATIC LEADERSHIP, IDEALIZATION, SAFEGUARDING AND GOVERNANCE

The sudden closure of the charity Kids Company was headline news in the UK on 6 August 2015. In this piece the author shares her feeling of shock, her questions and her concerns arising from the BBC interviews with the charity's founder Camila Batmanghelidjh who had been at the helm for 19 years. While alluding to the vision of charismatic leaders and their extraordinary ability to bring about social transformations, the author refers to Weber and others highlighting that charismatic leadership must be transitional if the enterprise is to survive. However, charisma can lead to idealization which puts the enterprise at risk.

Casey Schwartz

Casey Schwartz   Writer in New York. In the Mind Fields: Exploring the New Science of Neuropsychoanalysis, published in 2015 by Pantheon, is her first book. Her writing has also appeared in the New York Times and Newsweek, among other publications. A graduate of Brown University, she also holds a Master's degree in Psychodynamic Developmental Neuroscience from University College London.

‘What do you mean you haven't read Oliver Sacks?’ This was a conversation taking place in a fourth-floor walk-up apartment, whose every wall was lined with books, in Brooklyn, New York, springtime 2013.I faced my interlocutor - a teacher of English literature - wordlessly. There was nothing to say. Simply put, my failure to have investigated anew the writings of the legendary English neurologist was an absurdity, considering that at that moment, my life was consumed with the struggle to write a book that more than trenched on Sacksian territory, a book about the emerging field of neuropsychoanalysis, a book that involved, in part, the story of a man who, after a stroke, had lost the ability to speak.

My host - I shall call him Chris N. - promptly reached towards the shelf above his head and pulled down - what else? - The Man who Mistook his Wife for a Hat, Sacks’ early, classic collection of case studies. After a moment's consideration, Chris N. flipped to the essay entitled ‘The Lost Mariner’ and, with his perfectly fitting English accent, began aloud:

It immediately made me think of a patient of mine in whom these questions are precisely exemplified: charming, intelligent, memoryless Jimmy G., who was admitted to our Home for the Aged near New York City early in 1975, with a cryptic transfer note saying, ‘Helpless, demented, confused and disoriented.’

‘My state exactly’, I put in, an instant testament to one of Sacks’ most profound gifts: to let his readers identify with the very people we might otherwise see as quite alien, quite other. In his hands, they become familiar again. Sacks had now entered my life, and would soon become a muse, a guide, and even a moral compass.

Oliver Sacks grew up in a North London world where accomplishment was the norm and the expectation. His parents were both doctors; indeed, his mother was one of the first female surgeons in England. Sacks himself would, by the end of his life, have essentially created a new genre of literature: what he himself described as ‘the neurological novel’. Which is to say, he wrote about real life patients as a novelist would, relishing the specifics of each person, passionately invested in their details.

Joseph Schwartz  

The US novelist, Bernard Malamud, once wrote that all biography is ultimately fiction, a fair enough statement from one of the most distinguished novelists of his generation provided we understand fiction simply as a story. So what kind of a story has Joseph Berke given us in his account of a hidden Freud?

In the first instance it is an amusing, even profound, turning of Marx on his head. Instead of religion as a defence against the realities of materialism - the soul of soulless conditions - Berke tells a story of Freud using materialism as a defence against the Hassidic religion in which he was raised. It is a pretty good story that will especially appeal to readers who have a taste for psychohistory. It is interesting to see how much of psychoanalysis Berke can trace to roots in Jewish mysticism.

His account of Jewish mysticism is rich and informed.

Helena Bassil-Morozow

[hbassilmorozow@googlemail.com]

Helena Bassil-Morozow  

This brilliant retrospective collection goes back nearly 20 years and includes all the subjects that became the hallmark of Andrew Samuels's work: family and gender in the twenty-first century, the boundary between the political and the psychological, the social role of the therapist, the question of morality in a pluralist society, politics and rebellion, the psychology of the capitalist system, and the vexed question of Jung's anti-Semitism.

All these disparate themes in Passions, Persons, Psychotherapy, Politics are united by the concern for the individual in today's globalized, fluid world in which identities are more fragmented than ever, and the weakened community structures and family ties are no longer capable of providing human beings with the emotional support and dependable ‘rules for living’. So today's individuation is a tricky affair and is very different from what it used to be even in Jung's time. Individual freedom comes with a price, and this price is choice - availability of options, opinions, moralities, and ways of living.

This choice, this a-systemic, tricksterish plurality can be experienced as either exciting and liberating or depressing and even tragic.

Rozsika Parker Prize 2016

Rozsika Parker, author of Torn in Two: The Experience of Maternal Ambivalence and The Subversive Stitch: Embroidery and the Making of the Feminine, represented WPF/FPC on the BJP's Board for many years. She remained a member of the Journal's Editorial Advisory Panel until her death in 2010. She was well known for her commitment to creativity, in both art and clinical practice, and our annual Prize, established in 2013, focuses on a critical engagement with this theme. The Journal is particularly interested in factors that support creativity in clinical or theoretical work, and those that may militate against it. In addition to the focus on creativity, the application of psychoanalytic theory to questions of gender; the arts; and social and cultural themes is welcomed. Authors should consult the BJP's submission guidelines (particularly in relation to confidentiality, where clinical material is concerned) and prepare their work with the Journal's Aims and Scope statement in mind. Advice will be available for questions concerning confidentiality, or eligibility to submit work.

The Prize has two entry routes: a Student Path and a Post-Qualification Path. Students or qualified clinicians are invited to submit original (ie unpublished) papers on adult, child, couple, or group psychotherapy or psychoanalysis, on clinical, theoretical, applied or research topics. The Student path is open to students on an initial clinical training, who are either currently in training or who have qualified within the last 12 months; and to students on university courses in psychoanalytic studies, and on university courses where psychoanalysis is a significant component. A student paper may have been submitted as part of a course requirement, if this is acceptable to the student's course, but the paper should be revised as need be to meet the criteria of this Prize. The Post-Qualification path is open to clinically qualified individuals only. Papers should be singly authored, but due acknowledgement should be made if the work is based on a joint project.

Editor's Comments

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

[bjp@ann-scott.net]

Ann Scott  

I recently mentioned a meeting with the Journal's Reviewing Panel designed to help us consider priorities for the next period, ‘and to look at how we can enhance the Journal’ (BJP 31(4), November 2015, p. 417). It is appropriate that two such enhancements are represented in this issue, at the start of the year and of a new volume. One is signalled at the end of these Comments. Under the heading ‘New Writers/New Voices’ we are inviting ‘the next generation of psychotherapists’ to put forward work for publication. We hope that readers who have perhaps not published before, or are at an early stage of their clinical career, will see the BJP as a receptive space for the development of their ideas, and of a distinctive personal voice. The other is a development of the BJP's role as a journal for theoretical innovation. In a significant theoretical intervention in the psychoanalytic debate on morality, Coline Covington considers whether there may be ‘an idea of “right” and “wrong” that precedes the tenets of the group’, proposing that our sense of morality is based on our ‘initial perception of ourselves, as mirrored by the observing ego’.

A subtle interweaving of clinical and theoretical considerations links the next four papers. Detailed and evocative clinical material is included in each one. Federica Facchin considers ‘fuzzy contemporary clinical phenomena’ - those that defy traditional classification - in terms of Lacan's classical teaching on neurosis and psychosis, and contemporary Lacanian theories focused more on the notions of ‘jouissance, suppletion and ordinary psychosis’. Gilly Stiffell and Ralph Holtom contrast the classical perception of narcissism, in which ‘total disregard is shown for others’, with the ‘obverse position where the narcissist seems to be seeking relatedness by making seductive efforts to attract others into collusion with their needs’. They focus their discussion on the latter. Rooting his discussion of work with schizoid patients in material from a long-term treatment, Noel Hess poses ‘the difficult question … as to how much progress is possible’. There can be a risk (as in any analytic treatment), he argues, of ‘extending treatments beyond a point at which they are useful’, but he thinks the danger is more present in this patient group because of the nature of their transference. Nina Tamas extends the discussion of the psychic retreat by drawing attention to ‘the pre-symbolic processes that could form the basis from which the symbolic content of the psychic retreat develops’, and ‘secondary dissociative states of which psychic retreats constitute a distinctive class’.

The Effects of Opposite-Sex Twinship on the Adult Twin

Oliver Shirley

Oliver Shirley

[oliver@shirleyassoc.freeserve.co.uk]

Oliver Shirley   Honours degree in English, a Masters degree in Psycho-Social Studies and diplomas in Agriculture and Management Studies. Now retired, he was formerly a freelance management consultant for third-sector organizations and also an MSc tutor in Engineering Management at the University of Bristol. His research interests have included the effects of problem debt on mental health and the effects of opposite-sex twinship on the life of the adult twin - both topics approached from a psycho-social perspective.
ADULT MENTAL HEALTH, INDIVIDUATION, IDENTITY, OPPOSITE-SEX TWINS, PSYCHOSOCIAL RELATIONSHIPS, CLEAVING TO CO-TWIN

In this small-scale indicative study I explored the issue of individuation in relation to the life stories of a group of adult opposite-sex twins, using a psycho-social approach and a narrative interview methodology (Hollway & Jefferson, 2013). I found that none of the six interviewees reported having had a close relationship with their mother in infancy and childhood but five said they had had a close relationship with their co-twin, which endured in later life. Cleaving to the co-twin seemed to complicate and disrupt identity formation and the development of mature adult relationships. I concluded that the respondents in the study had experienced a similar psycho-social challenge to that of same-sex twins - how to honour their twinship while at the same time attempting to forge a unique identity - but that they seemed to have faced an additional challenge when it came to developing adult relationships with members of the opposite sex.

Janet Sayers

Janet Sayers

Emeritus Professor of Psychoanalytic Psychology
University of Kent
[j.v.sayers@kent.ac.uk]

Janet Sayers  

The visit by Freud and Jung to the USA in 1909 was followed in the 1920s by psychoanalytic ideas becoming ubiquitous there. Psychoanalytic ideas became even more ubiquitous in the USA after the arrival there of psychoanalysts from Europe before the Second World War. Yet, after the war, psychoanalytic ideas in the USA were dealt a body blow by Hans Eysenck, says Rutgers professor of psychology and philosophy, Robert Woolfolk.

On the basis of summing up a number of studies, Eysenck (1952) reported that while 72% of patients improved without psychoanalytic or non-psychoanalytic psychotherapy only 44% of psychoanalytically treated patients and 64% of non-psychoanalytically treated patients improved. There were problems, however, with Eysenck's method of summing up the results of different studies of the effects of psychoanalysis and psychotherapy. As a result it was widely agreed that Eysenck had failed to validate his critique of psychoanalysis and psychotherapy.

Eysenck was not their only critic. Further criticism came from the ‘biomedical psychiatry revolution’ which reinstated the assumption that ‘mental illnesses are brain diseases’ (p. 41). This revolution was evident, argues Woolfolk, when the American Psychiatric Association replaced its 1968 Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-II) with a 1980 manual (DSM-III) which, instead of diagnosing mental disorders in terms of psychoanalytic theories about their causation, diagnosed these disorders on the basis of their presenting symptoms. This includes, in its latest edition (DSM-V), absurdly diagnosing ‘grief following a bereavement, if it lasts longer than a couple of months, as a mental disorder’ (Forrester, 2015, p. 32).

Yet the DSM continues to be used in selecting patients for inclusion in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in which the effect on mental disorders of drug company products is compared with the effect of psychotherapy and cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT). Validated by RCTs, the pharmacology industry was confident by the 1990s, says Woolfolk, that it had discovered cures for most mental illnesses.

Ann Scott

Ann Scott  

In my last Comments I mentioned the BJP's new emphasis on its role as a journal for theoretical innovation. We consolidate in this issue with an adjustment to our Aims and Scope statement, agreed at a recent meeting of the Journal's Editorial Board (see opposite). We have traditionally said: ‘We welcome theoretical papers’. We are now saying that ‘We welcome theoretical papers, especially where there is theoretical innovation’ (my italics), and hope this will encourage readers to offer work which develops psychoanalytic thinking of this kind.

Relatedly, an adjustment to the Journal's usual section heading ‘Clinical Practice’, now ‘Clinical and Theoretical Practice’, underlines the importance of a dialectic between clinical and theoretical thinking. This dialectic is illustrated in the first two papers in the issue. Alistair Sweet and Ian Miller address an importantly under-theorized area of the addictions, ‘bingeing on sobriety’ - periods of abstinence which ‘may also represent a type of binge-like behaviour which satisfies, for a time, core needs’, and which they discuss in terms of black and white holes, locating their discussion in terms of earlier uses of these terms in the analytic literature. Sharon Gil, in a candid clinical account, looks at the paradox of a therapeutic relationship where there is a history of sexual abuse: how can therapeutic relatedness ‘sustain maternal concern when, at the same time, the therapeutic couple is unconsciously forced to re-enact elements of an unforgiving past?’ Winnicott's distinction between concern of guilt and concern of joy provides an overarching framework for Gil's discussion.

An understanding of mentalization, both as theoretical development and as clinical practice, was the theme of a recent joint conference between the Freud Museum and the Journal; I introduce the conference papers later in the issue (pp. 187-8). Here I want to acknowledge the importance of the Journal's link with the Museum. Joint conferences between us go back to the 1990s and it is a pleasure to revive and renew them now.

Introduction

Ann Scott

Ann Scott

[bjp@ann-scott.net]

Ann Scott  

The BJP's joint conference with the Freud Museum, London in November 2015 marked the renewal of an early collaborative project in the Journal's history, going back to the 1990s. It is a pleasure to be working closely again on the planning of a conference with Ivan Ward, Deputy Director and Director of Learning at the Museum; and to have the backing of Carol Siegel, Director of the Freud Museum, along with the active support of the British Psychotherapy Foundation, co-owner of the BJP, for the project as a whole. This initial conference, ‘Mentalization and the Unconscious’, marked the first in a series of annual events to be held over the next period. Our aim is to explore issues which are live and meaningful in contemporary clinical, professional and cultural debate.

‘Mentalization and the Unconscious’ took place within the Freud Museum's Festival of the Unconscious, a revisiting, in different media, of Freud's seminal paper of 1915, ‘The unconscious’. This was a paper that James Strachey, Freud's translator and editor, has said was written in less than three weeks (Strachey, 1957, p. 161). As the Museum's website put it, the existence of unconscious processes in the mind was recognized long before Freud, but:

What Freud introduced was the revolutionary notion of a dynamic unconscious, working in a different way from consciousness, with its own kind of logic… in which certain ideas are hidden from conscious awareness but continue to motivate our behaviour. He established ‘the unconscious’ as the principal object of psychoanalysis and the key term of its theory.

The conference sought to keep this ‘principal object’ in mind as the speakers considered the origins and development of the concept of mentalization, and its influential place in contemporary psychoanalysis - both theoretically and in terms of therapeutic practice.1 Each of the speakers, from their individual perspective, creatively addressed these questions, implicitly or explicitly. Four of the five main papers are published in this issue of the BJP; Peter Fonagy's clinical presentation will be published in the International Journal of Psychoanalysis (Fonagy and Allison, 2016, in press). Sometimes the focus was fairly and squarely on the concept of mentalization itself - its language and terms of reference, its reach, its clinical application - as in Catherine Freeman and Mary Target's contributions; sometimes on a different approach within psychoanalysis which might contribute to our thinking about mentalization, as in Nicola Abel-Hirsch's consideration of Bion's alpha-function;2

PRISON, ETHICAL DILEMMAS, VIOLENCE, SEXUAL HOSTILITY, OEDIPAL REALITY

The author describes the experience of undertaking psychotherapy with highly defended patients in the context of a prison cell in a London prison, rather than her customary private practice. She presents an ethical challenge to psychotherapists to enhance the quality of their private work by stepping outside the familiarity of the consulting room into contexts which involve change, challenge and subsequent clinical development. The author highlights theories around violence and the sexualization of aggression and describes the demand of ‘in the moment’ ethical challenges present in work with two patients, one convicted for child abuse and the other for rape. The paper also raises questions around how the aggression inherent in the prison system leads to the perpetuation of offending, and how psychotherapy allowed the patients to begin to work through their histories enveloped in their offences.

Mary Campbell  

Dr Suzanne O'Sullivan, consultant neurologist at the Queen Square National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery in London, is the author of this intriguing and important book, which has been shortlisted for the Wellcome Book Prize 2016. Her case histories read rather like another book of case histories more familiar to psychoanalysts and psychotherapists published 120 years ago - Freud and Breuer's Studies in Hysteria. O'Sullivan writes about the many patients in her practice who suffer from various forms of hysteria, within which term we might today include medically unexplained symptoms (MUS), psychosomatic disorders, functional disorders, dissociative seizures or conversion disorder.

‘It's all in your head’ - a familiar and dismissive remark when someone is thought to be imagining things. The words ‘true’ and ‘imaginary’ in the subtitle face the reader with a contradiction. The author writes of her experiences as a neurologist with patients referred for various, often dramatic, symptoms such as blindness, paralysis, seizures, chronic fatigue, intense pain, Munchausen syndrome. My reading of the title is that what is ‘true’ refers to the reality of painful symptoms her patients are undergoing, while the ‘imaginary’ refers to how their symptoms are interpreted by the doctor and others. Following the barrage of medical tests which inevitably and rightly precede and follow the initial appointment with the consultant neurologist, the patients described by O'Sullivan are the ones whose test results come back ‘normal’. No organic cause found. She writes about symptoms which have no apparent or identifiable physical or neurological cause or disease. She writes about the patients who still suffer from these symptoms and who come to her for help, or at the very least a medical diagnosis.

What I find tantalizing is that the author's account of her involvement with each patient seems to end where psychotherapy might begin. Like Freud, O'Sullivan writes with a mixture of curiosity, compassion, exasperation and generosity towards her patients and their unusually puzzling and often severe forms of physical suffering. Unlike Freud, who started out as a neurologist but moved on to develop his radical metapsychology which would later become known as psychoanalysis, O'Sullivan continues to work at the coal face of neurology, so to speak, where patients are seeking medical help to explain, treat and hopefully cure their usually painful, disabling and distressing symptoms.

Jeremy Holmes  

Psychotherapists have a unique vantage point on the vicissitudes of contemporary intrapsychic and interpersonal life. There can be few of us who have not found ourselves perturbed by the sight of groups of people - in railway carriages, walking with their families down the street, sitting side by side in a café - gazing raptly at their smartphones, or talking into them, rather than interacting with the environment, human and non-human, with which we are surrounded. Does this signify the increasing autism and isolation of modern life, a withdrawal from connectedness and communication? Or should it be celebrated as a manifestation of the ‘global village’ and of how modern technology enables us to remain psychically in touch with the significant people and attachment figures in our lives, however physically far apart? Can Freud's famous telephone metaphor of the unconscious of the analyst resonating with that of the patient, be ‘back-translated’ into the reality of the voice of a loved one in one's ear as a true manifestation of attachment and love?

One of the enduring strengths of attachment theory is its capacity to encompass both the evolutionary origins of human behaviour, and at the same time to pinpoint the role of context and the contemporary in shaping attachment patterns. Bowlby and Hinde coined the phrase the Environment of Evolutionary Adaptiveness to describe the selection pressures which influenced the origins of the attachment dynamic: the role of the infant-parent attachment bond as a protection from predation in a hostile environment, and later as the glue that holds couples, families and societies together. Meanwhile, Mikulincer and Shaver (2007) show how subliminal exposure to attachment-related words - ‘love’, ‘mother’, ‘home’ etc. - help the insecurely attached move to more secure dispositions, better able to describe and resolve interpersonal conflict, and less prone to chauvinism and suspicion.

In this timely volume, Cundy and her fellow attachment-oriented co-authors tackle the problems and opportunities thrown up for therapists by the digital age - how our stone-age psyches are both liberated and seduced by email, internet, social media, skype, twitter, instagram and no doubt other strange realms beyond your elderly reviewer's cyber-comprehension.

The Journal is delighted to mark the return of its Clinical Commentaries with this issue. The presentation of detailed, sessional material with close commentaries by clinicians of different orientations was one of the early initiatives of the Journal, and the section ran, as Mark Budden and Ann Horne remind us in their editorial introduction to this issue's Commentary, for over twenty years, with a total of 35 Commentaries in all. From the outset the section ‘attracted a good deal of interest’ (Hinshelwood, 1986, p. 254). It chimed in with the Journal's explicit commitment to debate from different analytic perspectives, its capacity to encompass ‘wide variations in the approach to the mind and its peculiarities’, a variation which Hinshelwood hoped was becoming a ‘recognised and enjoyable feature of our Journal’ (p. 254). In reviving the section now, we are maintaining the original format of the Commentaries, marking this with continuity of numbering. In this issue, Commentary 36 presents a clinical situation in which the therapist is ‘not allowed to be someone who matters' to the patient. I want to acknowledge our Editorial Board members Mark Budden and Ann Horne, who have worked skilfully to prepare the material for publication and who will be editing the Commentaries in future issues.

In this issue we are also delighted to publish the winning papers from the third year of the Rozsika Parker Prize. Caroline Ballinger (Birkbeck, London) was awarded the 2015 Student Prize for her close study of Bion's war writing, suggesting that Klein's concept of unconscious reparation may be helpful in considering Bion's life and work during this period. Her meticulous account shows deep engagement with her source material. Judith Mitrani (Los Angeles and Paris) was awarded the 2015 Post-Qualification Prize for her vivid clinical study of work with a female patient whose painstaking and at times turbulent development of a psychic skin evolved alongside the development of her fine art photography. We hope that readers will be able to join us for the two presentation events at which the authors will read and discuss their work (see Save the Date, p. 299).

I read this material on the day I heard the psychotherapist, Susie Orbach, on the radio, in imaginary conversation with a ‘patient’ who declared his love for her and expressed his wish to spend the rest of his life with her. I thought of how the patient in this clinical material comes from the opposite end of the spectrum!

We are not clear whether this is a male or female therapist working with this young, well defended and resistant female patient. We are told that this is a once a week treatment, which has been in place for over two years. We are not told why this has become established; whether a more frequent therapy has been discussed, which might well, I suppose, have been rejected by this patient who is so terrified of anything pertaining to intimacy. I would hope that the therapist might be working with a more frequent model in mind and wondering all the time about the patient's resistance.

I get a sense of two people struggling to make contact and understand each other. She sought therapy ‘due to feeling depressed and anxious and unable to sustain a relationship’. The therapist chooses her material to discuss because s/he does not feel protective of her as s/he does with other patients; and later in the presentation, feels annoyed with her for arriving early, and recognizes that her tone stirs up some irritation in him/her; and at the end reports feeling ‘frustrated and somewhat hopeless’. Here is a therapist who can be honest about countertransference feelings, both negative and positive, and about how they shift during the session; and who can think about the transference/countertransference dynamics in a way that must be helpful to his/her patients as well as to this commentator. However, in once a week work it is so very difficult to work at any depth with any but the most psychoanalytically minded patient.

Andrea Sabbadini  

In 1979 I had the memorable experience of attending a series of seminars that Wilfred Bion, then in his eighties, was giving at the Tavistock Clinic a few months before his death. These were structured, or should I say unstructured, in such a way as to represent and convey a sense of what some psychoanalytic sessions could feel like to patients and analysts alike: dominated by the logic of Primary Process functioning, a sense of timelessness, occasionally with an apparent lack of narrative beyond a free associative one, flooded with undigested proto-emotions, perhaps more similar to lived-out dreams than to the cultural events we expected those seminars to be. This uncanny sort of reverie experience, at least for many of us in the audience, was both surprising (we expected to be told about psychoanalysis, not to find ourselves immersed into it!) and also, I must confess, quite infuriating.

Torments of the Soul, originally published in Italy in 2010 and recently brought out by Routledge in a good English translation by Ian Harvey, has provoked in me similar reactions to those I had felt at the Tavistock so many years ago. This is no coincidence, since the book's author, the prominent Sicilian psychoanalyst Antonino Ferro, was much influenced by Bion: by his theories, such as those about reverie, alpha function and beta elements, as well as by his very ‘philosophy’ of what psychoanalytic work should be about. Chapter nine of Ferro's book, entitled ‘Clinical implications of Bion's thinking’, clarifies his relationship to his English mentor.

Ferro, of course, is not just a ‘Bionian’: his often controversial views ‘at the cutting edge’ of psychoanalysis, as James Grotstein writes in the Preface to the book, have also been shaped by his extensive reading of many other analytic authors, in particular Grotstein himself, Ogden, the Barangers and the Botellas. But there is no doubt that Bion's personality, as well as his key theoretical and clinical concepts, dominate Ferro's understanding of the work of psychoanalysis, of its structure and of its function - as will be apparent to anyone reading this book, or any of his numerous earlier ones.

As another volume of the BJP is completed, it is a pleasure to note the trends that we are seeing. The number of original submissions has increased by approximately 40% in the last year. This increase is paralleled by a comparable increase in the number of peer reviewers whose expertise we have called on, and whose names are acknowledged, with our appreciation, in this issue. A higher proportion of our peer reviewers in the last twelve months have come from organizations that are represented on the Board of the BJP or who have been recommended to us by our longstanding reviewers; we hope that this development adds to the coherence and robustness of our clinical and conceptual framework. In addition, the proportion of international submissions continues to rise, something that we have seen since the BJP went into PEPweb nearly three years ago. This welcome trend is perhaps illustrated in the diverse provenance of the papers in this issue.

In a wide-ranging, scholarly study of ‘Janet vs Freud’ on traumatization - the theory of structural dissociation vs a psychoanalytic model of the mind - Joan Lesley and Sverre Varvin (Oslo) argue that ‘both the conceptualization of the human being and the understanding of traumatization and treatment’ differ in the two models. Through complex clinical examples, they show how an alternative, ‘uniquely individual understanding of the patient is achieved by following the transference and countertransference that must necessarily determine the direction of the therapeutic process’. Massimiliano Sommantico (Naples) addresses unconscious communication within the couple, especially through the means of dreams. As he says, ‘a dream in couple psychoanalytic psychotherapy reveals individual states of mind, but at the same time it expresses a joint psychic organization’. The patients are a married couple in their early forties, with four children, the eldest of whom has Down's syndrome. Rooted in a survey of different theoretical approaches to couple work, the paper offers a detailed and subtle clinical exploration of a family crisis prompted by the husband's infidelity.

Alison Lee

Alison Lee

alisonlee62@hotmail.com

Alison Lee   Psychoanalytic psychotherapist in private practice in Oxfordshire. She completed a DPhil in English Literature before training with the Scottish Institute of Human Relations. She has taught on the Scottish Training in Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy and also for the North Eastern Association of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy.
Female Friendship, Rivalry, Lateral Relationships, Creativity

In this paper female-to-female friendship as depicted in the Neapolitan novels of Elena Ferrante is used to think about aspects of unconscious relating, and of feminine identity. The two girls in the stories ‘blur’ into one another, in a way that is at times a source of creative strength, and at times a quasi-psychotic state. The idea of ‘merger’ as characterizing female relationships is considered through the narrative. Friendship stands outside conventional psychoanalytic models of family relating, but Ferrante explores their internal workings, particularly in the developing child and adolescent, and unfolds the importance of their place in growing up, asserting a unique psychic place for the female-to-female bond in identity formation. Psychoanalytic ideas of separation and individuation are brought to bear, alongside Juliet Mitchell's work on sibling relationships, and Rozsika Parker's work on the internal ‘other’ necessary for creativity.

Jyoti Smith

jysmith@aut.ac.nz

Jyoti Smith   Psychotherapy works as a psychotherapist, group facilitator and family therapist at Higher Ground, an Auckland-based therapeutic community for alcoholics and drug addicts. In her private practice, she offers supervision to other counsellors/psychotherapists and works with adults struggling with a range of challenges, including addictions.
Sandtray, Sandplay, Trauma, Adult Clients, Safety, Communication, Thematic Analysis, Nightmares

In work with adult trauma survivors the therapeutic relationship can become highly charged with trauma-related transferential dynamics, placing severe strain on the therapist and potentially resulting in vicarious traumatization. This article reports on the findings of a thematic analysis of the literature on the use of sandtray when working with adult trauma survivors. The research confirms the benefits of using sandplay work as it increases safety for client and therapist, fosters communication of the often ‘unspeakable’ experience of trauma and, as a result of the activity involved in sandtray work, provides experiences of empowerment for the client, thus facilitating healing from traumatic experiences.

This is a very impressive book, of great interest to any reader who is a psychotherapist (and indeed those who are not), for many different reasons.

Firstly, In the Mind Fields is a beautifully constructed narrative, scaled over a decade, of a young woman coming to terms with the apparently distinctive universes of brain and mind. In taking the world's first formal Masters course linking psychoanalysis with the neurosciences, Schwartz is exposed to novel psychotherapeutic concepts (novel at least to her), to parts of the brain she is unfamiliar with, and to cutting edge neuroscientific technologies. Reading of her personalized encounters was entertaining as well as educational. But the book is also a narrative of other journeys - between University College London and Yale (where her cross-continental Masters course is boldly co-convened), to the imposing world of the New York Psychoanalytic Institute, and indeed to a wine farm in Southern Africa. Even if it were not a book about a very modern science, it would be a fascinating Paul Theroux-style travel narrative. But, in the way that good education in the mental sciences can be, the book is also a journey of the soul - as the themes of her formal work intersect with the mental health issues in her family, and with her developing understanding of the mind. For these reasons, the book would be a good read even for the non-therapist.

Secondly, the book is a narrative around a developing field: neuropsychoanalysis. This is a discipline in which I have played a modest role over the years - but I have had no link with the writing of the book, so I read an outsider's account of my home turf with fascination. Schwartz's view of the inter-discipline is, on the one hand, of a vibrant and exciting set of bridges - between what initially seem to her to be the radically different disciplines of brain and mind. Gradually, she comes to realize that these are really just two perspectives on a single phenomenon (for more on this dual-aspect monist approach, see Solms & Turnbull, 2011, or 2002, Chapter 2). Joseph Friel

joe74a@gmail.com

Joseph Friel   Qualified and accredited counselling psychotherapist working within the public sector and in his private practice based in the northwest of Ireland. He gained an MA in Psychology from the University of Aberdeen in 2000. In 2005 he completed a Post Graduate Certification in Integrative Psychotherapy and subsequently a Diploma in Suicide Studies in 2010. In 2013 he completed an MSc in Integrative Psychotherapy. He is a member of the British Psychological Society, a graduate of the Sherwood Psychotherapy Training Institute in Nottingham, and an accredited member of both the Irish Association for Counselling & Psychotherapy (IACP) and the UK Council for Psychotherapy (UKCP).
Shame, Toxic Shame, Integrative Psychotherapy, Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis, Regression, Attachment, Reparative Relationship

This study investigated the detoxification process of shame in integrative psychotherapy from the client's perspective, focusing on the experience of shame and the interventions used in working with toxic shame. Through identifying the detoxification process, successful therapeutic outcomes that reduced shame over time were determined with further exploration into the experience of the shame phenomenon. Interpretative phenomenological analysis was used to analyse data from transcripts of semi-structured recorded interviews from a sample of trainee/qualified therapists who had experienced shame as clients. The findings from the study evidence the separating and isolating qualities of the shame experience, an experience that was crippling and correlated with development and early infantile relationships. The findings of this study highlight how shame is experienced and the fundamental role therapists have in detoxifying shame through recognizing, understanding and working to normalize it. Sensitivity to the shame experience is crucial so as not to compound the shame experience further. The need to be sensitive to regression in treatment, the need for a secure attachment within a relational oriented psychotherapy such as integrative psychotherapy and the centrality of the relationship in the reparative process are seen as fundamental to the effective management of toxic shame. In view of integrative psychotherapy being influenced by a variety of psychoanalytical theories, this paper draws upon psychoanalytic and humanistic perspectives in the analysis and interpretation of the findings.

Peter Wilson  

This book is about boarding schools and their impact on the emotional lives of their pupils - not just the immediate impact as it occurs in childhood and adolescence but also far reaching as it extends into the thinking, attitude and behaviour of adults many years later. The author has written a compelling account inspired largely by her growing psychoanalytic practice with adults whose depressed states turn out to have derived from the consequences of their boarding school life. Out of all this, she has produced a truly exhaustive study of the nature of boarding schools, the vulnerabilities of children and the powerful emotional residues of early experience seeped in the ways of boarding school life. It is far from a rosy picture; more a tragic story of emotional blight.

The independent Schools Council (ISC) report for 2013 recorded 66,776 pupils boarding in 465 ISC schools. This constituted 13.1 per cent of total pupil numbers. ‘What is so extraordinary about the statistics is that those attending boarding schools are a minority - yet in government most of the policy makers are ex-boarders. They are also represented in all the major institutions in Britain’ (p. 4). This is an important political point, highlighting the pervasive influence of a certain kind of upbringing on the mentalities of those in leadership positions in our society: ‘The social implications of boarding school are based on a patriarchal tradition that runs like a fault line, an unseen influence, in British society. An outcome of early boarding may be that children have to learn to cut themselves off from compassion for their own predicament’ (p. 10).

The author proposes the idea of a mental phenomenon to be known as boarding school syndrome. Her intention is not to pathologize all who have attended boarding school; nor is she seeking to establish a new category of mental disorder. Rather she is wanting to alert us to the fact that there ‘is an identifiable cluster of learned behaviours and emotional states that may follow growing up in a boarding school … it is the pattern that is discernible’ (p. 2, emphasis in the original).

NARCISSISM, SEDUCTIVE, SIRENS, COUNTERTRANSFERENCE, ENACTMENT, DESTRUCTIVENESS

This paper is about narcissism and particularly about the paradoxical way in which some narcissists use objects. In the classical perception of narcissism total disregard is shown for others with the narcissist taking himself or his own reflection as his only object, yet we also encounter the obverse position where the narcissist seems to be seeking relatedness by making seductive efforts to attract others into collusion with their needs. This has not been widely discussed but we believe it represents a major division of narcissism with the classical disregard of others being replaced by a seductive drive for their subversion. This strategy is represented by the myth of the sirens who by the beauty of their song lured sailors to forget their own lives and ultimately fall to their destruction. We consider the sirens’ song and how the nature of its seductive lure is shaped by the therapist's own enactment in the countertransference. Previously narcissistic presentations have been thought of as movement along an axis of more or less grandiosity but we now propose that this concept is best broadened into a two-dimensional space where the second axis defines the degree of seduction employed.

David Mann  

This book is a welcome addition to the library on working with borderline personality disorder (BPD). The emphasis is on what the authors call transference-focused psychotherapy (TFP). Rooted in psychoanalytic thinking, the ambition of the book is to provide ‘a rigorous research methodology and empirical evaluation’. That objective is the strength of the book; in my view it is also its weakness.

TFP is designed for the most difficult patients in the therapist's case-load: patients presenting with BPD. In contrast to say, cognitive behavioural therapy, psychodynamic approaches not only offer symptom relief but also address the underlying structures of the BPD. The authors assert that TFP is a more systematic procedure for psychodynamic work with borderline patients. With that in mind, TFP initially promises to enhance the social and vocational functioning of the patient with BPD, their love lives and their creativity. Once the reader starts to dig deeper into the text, however, such sweeping statements start to be qualified.

The therapeutic treatment and application of TFP is broken down into stages: case selection, the importance of the frame, the development and analysis of the transference; guidelines are given for managing crises, sexual enactments, suicidal presentations and so forth. Indeed, the blurb on the back cover describes the book very well: ‘a remarkable roadmap for clinicians - truly a GPS for TFP that maps the treatment terrain’. In a nutshell, that is this book: it is a manual. Like all manuals, this means it has some useful information but also a lot of limitations.

The main components of BPD are commonly thought of as identity problems, negative relationships, affective instability and self-harm. Where the book is strong is with the excellent description of the internal world of the borderline patient. Psychodynamic conceptualizations have long emphasized that with BPD more needs to be taken into consideration than just the more observable behaviours. The subjective structures of BPD are best viewed in terms of the underlying psychological structures, which are usually less integrated. In normal personality organization, an individual has a more integrated sense of self and of significant others; he/she will have a broad spectrum of affective experiences, well modulated without loss of impulse control; there is usually an integrated system of internalized values, including a capacity for realistic self-appraisal and self-criticism.

A Couple's Unconscious Communication: Dreams

Massimiliano Sommantico

Massimiliano Sommantico

sommanti@unina.it

Massimiliano Sommantico   Clinical psychologist and a couple and family psychoanalytic psychotherapist. He is Aggregate Professor of Clinical Psychology in the Department of Human Studies, University of Naples, where he teaches fundamentals of psychoanalysis. He is a member of the Fourth Section (Psychoanalytic Couple and Family Psychotherapy) of the European Federation for Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy, and the Administration Council and the Scientific Council of the International Association of Couple and Family Psychoanalysis. He is also a member of the Séminaire Inter-Universitaire Européen d'Enseignement et de Recherche en Psychopathologie et Psychanalyse, and is a candidate of the Italian Psychoanalytic Society. He is particularly interested in working with couples and families, and his main clinical and research interests are in the field of individual, couple and family psychoanalysis, with particular interest in the fraternal dimension.
Couple Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy, Common and Shared Dream Space, Couple Associative Chain, Couple Linking, Inter-Phantasizing, Group Working-Through, ‘Therapeutic New Group’

The author describes the process of a couple's psychoanalytic psychotherapy, conducted in co-therapy, through the analysis of some dreams and their associations. The dream analysis will show the common and shared inter-subjective dimension of the couple that emerged from the psychoanalytic psychotherapy setting. Central notions of this clinical work are those of inter-phantasizing, common and shared dream space, and couple associative chain. But also the containing model of the psychic envelope can be considered as one of the bases of the theory of a couple's dream space. The author describes the process by which the partners of the couple, and more generally the ‘therapeutic new group’, were able to achieve the unveiling of a denial pact that allowed the couple to add to their family at the time of the birth of their first child with Down's syndrome; but also, and more fundamentally, what has allowed this young couple to cope with the trauma of this birth. The author finally shows how the group working-through, within the setting of the couple's psychoanalytic psychotherapy, gave new meaning to sensations, feelings and affects of the couple.

‘Janet vs Freud’ on Traumatization: A Critique of the Theory of Structural Dissociation from an Object Relations Perspective

Joan Lesley and Sverre Varvin MD DPhil

Sverre Varvin

joanlesley1@gmail.com

sverre.varvin@hioa.no

Sverre Varvin   Training and supervising analyst for the Norwegian Psychoanalytic Society and Professor at the Oslo and Akershus University College of Applied Sciences. He has been working clinically and in research on traumatization and the treatment of traumatized patients, especially in the refugee field. He has done process and outcome research on psychoanalytic therapy, research on traumatic dreams, and on psychoanalytic training, and has published several articles and books. He has twice been president of the Norwegian Psychoanalytic Society and he has held several positions at the International Psychoanalytical Association (IPA), among others, as vice president and board member. He is presently chair of the IPA China Committee.
Janet/Janetian, Freud/Freudian, Trauma/Traumatized/Traumatization, Theory of Structural Dissociation, Treatment/Therapy, Structural Dissociation, Object Relations, Transference, Countertransference

It is still ‘Janet vs Freud’. We present ‘The theory of structural dissociation’ and the three-phase treatment programme that provides the basis for treatment of traumatized patients in many services in Europe, exploring its shortcomings. With roots in Janet's work it displays a behaviouristic, systemic view of the human being that allows for an understanding of traumatic experience as preventing natural development of the personality towards an integrated unit, or disrupting integration, causing splits along fault lines between major personality systems. Traumatization, structural dissociation, produces patients with multiple inner parts, each with a subjective first person perspective of experience not (necessarily) shared with other parts. With our roots in Freud, from an object relations perspective, we illustrate, through clinical example with two traumatized female patients, how (1) the transference and countertransference provides a unique, alternative understanding of the traumatized patient determining the direction of the therapeutic process, thus making a phase-orientated therapy moot; (2) the patient's functioning prior to traumatization influences the actual traumatic experience, reactions to it and the treatment process; and (3) a patient's attachment needs and way of handling these, brings the traumatic experience into the treatment room from the first contact, providing a core process in the transference and countertransference throughout the therapy.

Nicola Abel-Hirsch   Fellow of the British Psychoanalytical Society and works in private practice. Her writings on Bion include: ‘Freud and Bion on the life instinct’, ‘Narcissism and socialism’, ‘Bion's containing and Winnicott's holding’, ‘Sexuality’, ‘On the difference between maternal reverie and analytic “alpha function’,” ‘The mind-body relation’, and ‘Bion on observation’. She is the editor of Hanna Segal's last book, Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow.
ALPHA-FUNCTION, UNCONSCIOUS, BETA, THINKING, DREAMING, FRUSTRATION, OMNISCIENCE

This paper will identify why and how Bion's ideas about dream-work and alpha-function evolved, and the profound implications of this development for what he calls ‘practical psychoanalysis’. Andre Green interestingly comments that for Bion the ‘model of the dream’ was unusually more important than the ‘model of the baby’; and I will consider in particular the question of ‘models’, and their relation to the making of the accurate observations of unconscious functioning we need to underpin our analytic work. It is hoped the paper will contribute to the clinically relevant question of whether there is an important link between Bion's ‘alpha-function’ and mentalization theory.

Jean-Paul Baldacchino BA (Hons) MA PHD

Jean-Paul Baldacchino

[jean-paul.baldacchino@um.edu.mt]

Jean-Paul Baldacchino   BA (Hons) (Melit) MA (VU) PhD (LaTrob) is an anthropologist who has conducted fieldwork in East Asia, the Native American Northwest, Australia and the Catholic Mediterranean. He maintains a research interest in the interface between culture and mental health. He studied psychoanalysis in the Lacanian tradition with the Australian Centre for Psychoanalysis. He obtained his Masters in Psychoanalysis (Clinical and Research) from Victoria University. He is currently Senior Lecturer in the Department of Anthropological Sciences at the University of Malta where he teaches psychoanalysis and anthropology. He has published in numerous journals on a variety of topics utilizing both anthropological and psychoanalytical perspectives. Clinically he is interested in dreams, emotions and the treatment of psychosis.
LACAN, PSYCHOSIS, HALLUCINATIONS, RELIGION, CULTURE, MALTA, THEOLOGY, ANTHROPOLOGY

Mysticism has long featured in discussions among psychoanalysts and mental health practitioners, anthropologists and scholars of religion. In this paper I analyse the life and visions of a twentieth century mystic in the Catholic Mediterranean. Through this case study I seek to compare the psychoanalytic and to a lesser extent the psychiatric discussions of ‘hallucinations’ with the theological explanations of visions. Via a Lacanian discussion of the case of the first Maltese saint I argue that there are interesting points of convergence between the two. An adequate understanding of the cultural context within which visions are articulated as meaningful experiences is essential to our understanding and clinical treatment of people presenting symptoms associated with religious content. A psychoanalytical understanding can serve to enrich and enliven theological discussions on madness as a path to sanctity.

Jocelyn Catty  

This collection of classic papers by Juliet Hopkins under the title An Independent Mind brings together a breadth and depth of thinking from across a fascinating professional career. As its editors, Ann Horne and Monica Lanyado, reflect in their Introduction, Juliet Hopkins's work has found an international audience among a wide range of professionals in child psychotherapy and psychology, child care, education and social care. They attribute this to three factors: her commitment to child development and improving practice; her ability to integrate a range of approaches; and her capacity to communicate in a clear and accessible way (p. xiv). The book benefits from a Foreword by Dilys Daws, who touchingly reflects on Hopkins's generosity to students and colleagues, and from a series of introductions by the editors to the collection as a whole and its grouped papers. Each group represents a key area of clinical practice; in each, Hopkins demonstrates her commitment to integrating different theoretical models and their associated practices. In offering such an integration, however, she never elides the differences between the theories and concepts under discussion, but rather brings out their particularities and the different ways in which they may illuminate the clinical picture. The reader never doubts that focus on the individual child or family lies at the heart of this careful thinking.

The first section, entitled ‘Trauma and child psychotherapy’, presents three papers about the role of trauma in the psychopathology of two young children, as well as the careful work that can be done to take ‘steps towards … recovery’ (p. 5). It is salutary, reading these papers today, to be reminded of the extent to which trauma was disregarded in earlier years. Lanyado writes:

When her paper was accepted for publication in 1984 the etiological importance of trauma was still so strongly denied that she had to appease the editor by amending her title from ‘The role of trauma’ to ‘The probable role of trauma’ (p. 3).

Psychiatry Core Trainees' Perception of Homophobia in Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy: A Preliminary Survey

Alexandros Chatziagorakis and Gearoid Fitzgerald

Gearoid Fitzgerald

40 Clarendon Road, Leeds LS2 9PJ, UK. [a.chatziagorakis@nhs.net]

Gearoid Fitzgerald   Psychoanalyst and consultant psychiatrist in psychotherapy at Leeds and York Partnerships NHS Foundation Trust. He is responsible for supervising core trainees in psychiatry and higher trainees in medical psychotherapy.
Homosexuality, NHS Psychotherapy, Psychiatry, Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy, Training

In 2009 the Royal College of Psychiatrists revised the curriculum for psychiatric training to include psychotherapy elements into the core curriculum. Trainees are now required to provide evidence of treating patients psychotherapeutically. The therapies that the trainees usually deliver are cognitive behavioural therapy and psychoanalytic psychotherapy (PAP). Psychoanalytic theory has largely viewed homosexuality as immaturity or pathology. Psychoanalytic theory and practice have traditionally been unable to incorporate homosexuality as a normal variant of sexuality and this has had significant consequences both for clinical practice and training. Our aim was to examine whether trainees have perceived their experience of PAP as homophobic. The study was done via an internet-based questionnaire survey. Simple descriptive statistics were used to analyse the results. Most trainees did not find PAP homophobic in theory, practice or supervision. A minority of trainees considered PAP as homophobic prior to undertaking a case and found it homophobic after undertaking a case. Some trainees found their experience of PAP has broadened their views on their sexuality. Participants’ experience was positive and PAP was not perceived as homophobic. A negative experience might have significant implications for their mental wellbeing, training and choice of future career.

Emma Letley

Emma Letley  

‘Screens display some of the thorniest, most complex set[s] of confusing questions I have encountered in a psychoanalytic career that has been connected to technology from the very beginning’. Thus writes Todd Essig, Training and Supervising Psychoanalyst from the William Alanson White Institute, New York, in the Foreword. Essig was an enthusiastic ‘adopter’ of the new technologies from the 1980s onwards. Having ‘charged online’ in the 1980s and set up The Psychoanalytic Connection in 1993, Essig then started to experience a growing ‘dystopian funk’. As most clinicians would recognize, books and screens are ‘wonderful Cartesian devices’; and yet, whilst they let us know what someone is thinking at a distance, we still wonder whether a Cartesian device is adequate, or to put it in Winnicottian terms (which Isaacs Russell so brilliantly does throughout this important book) good enough for our purposes. Whether or not there is ‘functional equivalence’, between co-present and mediated treatments, is a live and highly contentious issue, and Screen Relations comprehensively addresses so many of the issues involved recruiting not only psychoanalytic views but also input from the realms of neuroscience, information technology and cyberpsychology. Isaacs Russell is no Luddite and her examination of the issues surrounding screen relations is deep and deeply needed by all clinicians and others who operate through screen media.

She is a therapist who trained in the UK and moved to the USA and has a wealth of experience of remote clinical work, and a keen understanding of analytic therapy from Freud, Winnicott, Klein, Bion, Ogden and others. The questions motivating her text are those we should all ask ourselves before embarking on mediated work. They are: can an effective treatment proceed without physical presence? What happens in mediated treatment when there is no potential to ‘kiss or kick’? How is intimacy affected by altering the balance between implicit and explicit communications?

Dear Editor

I am writing to express my concern about the use of the term ‘analysis’ in the paper published in the August 2015 issue, ‘Hopelessness in the Analysis’. The therapeutic work referred to in this paper is once-weekly, which, as I understand it, is properly described as psychotherapy not psychoanalysis. I am aware of the considerable literature discussing the differentiation between psychotherapy and psychoanalysis, and while this is a controversial issue, I had understood that a defining feature of psychoanalysis is depth of emotional contact, made possible by a frequency of four or five sessions per week. I know it can be argued that equating depth of contact with a number (of session frequency) can seem arbitrary and simplistic, but in the main, we do, I think, assume that a relationship exists between frequency and intensity. I want to stress that I am not ascribing a value to either activity - I write as someone who practices both psychotherapy and psychoanalysis and view them as equally helpful. Nor am I criticising the content of this paper, which raises many interesting and important issues. My concern is with the misuse of the term ‘analysis’ in this paper. There is already considerable confusion in the mind of the public concerning the terms ‘therapy’ and analysis’, and I don't think it helps for us to add to that confusion.

Noel Hess

Building Concern Free of Force in the Treatment of Adult Survivors of Childhood Incest

Sharon Gil PHD

Sharon Gil

Mount Carmel, Haifa, Israel 31905. [gsharon@research.haifa.ac.il]

Sharon Gil   Clinical social worker, psychotherapist, and clinical supervisor; senior lecturer; head of the MA and supplementary programmes; and head of the unit for treating adult male survivors of sexual abuse.
INCEST, ADULT MENTAL HEALTH, ADULT PSYCHOTHERAPY, CASE STUDY, CHILD ABUSE

Incest brutally extinguishes the instinctive concern of a parent towards his/her child, transforming the relationship into one of force and destruction. This mode of communication tends to be re-enacted in therapy. A main paradox embodied in the treatment of adult survivors of incest is, therefore, the paradox of force and concern. How can therapeutic relatedness sustain maternal concern when, at the same time, the therapeutic couple is unconsciously forced to re-enact elements of an unforgiving past? By presenting clinical material, I demonstrate how this conflicting paradox blinded me while working with a female patient, leading us to an impasse, while overlooking and then re-enacting an incestuous relationship. In the process of re-enacting, maintaining genuine human concern was annihilated, as we both became figures in her previously written story. Concern free of force becomes possible when the therapeutic process is released from the burden of resolving the tension between concern and force, thereby gradually facilitating the evolution of a dialectical space that enables a more comprehensive mode of experience and communication. The force of abusive re-enactment, then, does not negate the free choice of the patient and the therapist alike to react to force with concern.

I explore the development of implicit mentalizing, its roots in internal working models of early attachment relationships and how these contribute to the emergence of epistemic trust. This essay draws on Winnicott's deep insights developed in a series of texts over the last decade of his life and addressing questions of gender and sexuality, as these phenomena shape and are shaped by core experiences in the evolution of intersubjectivity. Interweaving Winnicott's work with that of Loewald, Laplanche and Matte Blanco, the essay speculates about possible developmental processes through which complex and shifting gender identifications intersect and interact with experiences of sexuality and desiring. The essay tracks Winnicott's evolving ideas about gender and madness and opens a way of thinking about one process by which gender may emerge, in a complex, ‘softly assembled’ encounter with desire and being desired. This approach also seeks to reframe and expand the current move in gender theory ‘from etiology to teleology’. The term ‘etiology’ locates us in causation, diagnosis and the sites of pathology, and I think we should continue to be wary of the intrusion of these socially driven biases and ideas into reflections about sexuality and gender in development.

MENTALIZATION, BORDERLINE, MIRRORING, AFFECT REGULATION, INTENSIVE, INTERPRETATION, ATTACHMENT

The author discusses whether the concepts of mentalization are helpful within intensive, individual analytic work with a personality disordered patient. Child and adult technique within the widening scope of psychopathology can be thought of as building on developmental help, studied at the Anna Freud Centre from the sixties to reach ‘atypical’ children who could not use classical analysis. The first two years of work with Jenny, a young borderline woman, were anchored by developmental research on attachment and early parent-infant relating. Later, when her capacity to symbolize, tolerate and communicate affect had greatly improved, she could accept and use interpretations, and working in the transference was gradually able to be accepted as thinking and not only as action. The infantile modes of experiencing psychic reality hypothesized in mentalization theory are illustrated from the material, and the status of attachment within psychoanalytic theory is reconsidered. In the last section, how each psychotherapist specifically shapes the process of change will be discussed, building on the concept of ‘marked mirroring’.

This paper attempts to summarize the evolution of interest in the concept of mentalization which has been researched and enriched by the linking of many disciplines alongside that of psychoanalysis and attachment theory. Taking into account the work of Professors Fonagy and Target and many others, the paper describes factors that enable the development of the capacity to mentalize and those that interfere. It will consider how the quality of attachment affects the transformation of pre-mentalized modes of experience to the recognition of psychic reality of self and other. While mentalizing is part and parcel of all therapies, a mentalization-based therapy was developed in the context of treatment of borderline personality disorder patients by Professors Bateman and Fonagy. The paper will illustrate key concepts in the theory of mentalization with the vignette taken from clinical practice.

This article addresses Donald Winnicott's consistent attention to the idea of black and blackness as manifested in his work in the consulting room from the late 1940s to the 1960s. It describes several very different pieces, published and unpublished, where the use of black is recorded in patients’ material and the different directions they open up: skin colour, psychoanalytic research, representations of trauma and serious disturbance. Both Winnicott and this article argue for caution in ascribing any fixed connotation to black and blackness while recognizing its importance across cultures and historical epochs. In one of the articles under discussion, ‘Hallucination and dehallucination’ (1957), Winnicott refers to two male patients drawing with black pencil and I have linked his discussion both to the more general area of modern art and artists who have been interested in black and to contemporary psychoanalytic interest in unrepresented states. I emphasize the complexity of the arenas opened up by Winnicott and argue for their historical importance.

I am impressed and grateful to the therapist who made this thoughtful material available. (I am assuming that the writer is female.)

The therapist has chosen to write about a session with this patient, in part because she and the therapy are ‘not allowed to matter’ to the patient. Alone among her patients Holly doesn't elicit her protectiveness. The therapist, noticing this, examines the meaning of her countertransference, so singularly specific to this patient. She begins to reflect that not being allowed to matter is a central issue, unconsciously enacted by herself as well as by Holly. Perhaps she chooses to name her Holly in response to something tough and prickly about her.

The therapist recognizes the importance of the recurring dream in which Holly calls out from a bleak, desolate place but no one answers. The dream corresponds to Holly's experience of emotional neglect which is repeated by the lack of concern for her shown by her male partners. It is also re-evoked in the countertransference where the therapist has to endure having her importance disregarded and her overtures (like Holly's appeals in the dream) ignored. The therapist also has to suppress her anger at Holly's early arrival for the session and her cavalier disregard of how that might affect the therapist. Unconsciously Holly communicates to the therapist what it is like to be ignored and not to feel safe enough to be able to complain. She inquires implicitly how the therapist copes with this. Therapists are alert to the likelihood that they may be experienced as the parents were; they may, however, overlook what the patient projects into them of his or her own childhood suffering.

I wondered how this educated, single woman comes to be seen only once a week. I suspect it is the product of her need to control and limit her vulnerability. She sought therapy after the collapse of wedding plans but has tried to wipe out this trauma. She protects herself and does this so effectively that her therapist is lulled into overlooking the effect of her altering Holly's session time; she ‘buys into’ Holly's defence that these things don't matter. Perhaps Holly's lovers also ‘buy into’ it, failing to be thoughtful about what might be going on behind her compliance.

This is not an easy book to categorize, and by the end of reading it, categories come to feel irrelevant. In a little over 200 pages of this new edition, Andrew Lotterman manages to condense without reductionism, certain fundamental criteria for the understanding and treatment of people diagnosed with schizophrenia, using psychoanalytic and psychodynamic psychotherapeutic techniques. The first edition of the book was titled Specific Techniques for the Psychotherapy of Schizophrenic Patients, whereas this expanded edition updates research on the biology and psychology of psychosis and explores controversial issues surrounding diagnosis. It also includes two new chapters on the psychology and treatment of paranoia and on the experience of having a shattered self and the delusion of being the Messiah.

Adrian Stokes (1902-1972) was a British writer and painter, known principally as an influential art critic. He was also a published poet. Although Melanie Klein wrote about him as Mr B ‘a true homosexual’ (p. 265) in The Psychoanalysis of Children (1932), it was depression, not homosexuality or bisexuality, that led to analysis with her between 1929 and 1935, and again briefly in 1946. These analyses were followed by a sustained relationship with her and friendship with many of the talented Kleinian analysts of the time. Without developing an interest in psychoanalysis per se his understanding of the function and purpose of art was profoundly informed by his analysis. Richard Wollheim, the philosopher and editor of The Image in Form (1972), a selection of Stokes’ writings, observed that there seemed a ‘place reserved’ in Stokes’ mind for Melanie Klein's ideas. Stokes’ influence on contemporary culture was prodigious.
