Noel Hess

Noel Hess

Flat 4, Mullion Court, 112 Finchley Rd, London NW3 5JH. [noel.hess@candi.nhs.uk]

Noel Hess   Psychoanalytic psychotherapist (BPF) and psychoanalyst (BPA) in private practice and a consultant clinical psychologist in psychotherapy at Camden Psychotherapy Service, Camden & Islington NHS Foundation Trust.
SCHIZOID PERSONALITY, PSYCHOANALYTIC, COUNTERTRANSFERENCE, BION, NONRELATEDNESS

This paper describes and discusses those aspects of the treatment of schizoid patients which present particular challenges and difficulties to the clinician, namely nonrelatedness, emotional unavailability and absence of curiosity, all of which mean that the psychotherapist has a considerable strain to bear. Bion and others have suggested how the aetiology of this particular state of mind might be understood in terms of infantile experience. Clinical material from the long-term treatment of a schizoid man is discussed to illustrate how, in the course of a session, moments of meaningful emotional connection can become possible, and the transference/countertransference factors which might facilitate this. Implications for the length of treatment are discussed. The problem of overextending analytic therapies with this patient group is also discussed.

Helga Coulter   Psychoanalytic psychotherapist in private practice in Melbourne, Australia. She trained with the Lincoln Clinic and Institute for Psychotherapy and was a member until the merger with the British Psychotherapy Foundation in 2013/2014. Since 1993 she has been a member of the Victorian Association of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapists (Melbourne) where she was the Chair of Training and Chair of Professional Development. She teaches and supervises. She is particularly interested in the arts, a topic on which she has presented papers internationally and in Australia.
Käthe Kollwitz, Art, Expressionism, Totalitarian Art, Concept of ‘O’, Transformation, Psychoanalysis as an Art

The author's reaction to the sight of two of the works of the German expressionist artist Käthe Kollwitz on the walls of the rooms of her prospective training analyst forms the starting point for an exploration of art, totalitarianism and the art of psychoanalysis. The art and life of Kollwitz are used as the basis of an attempt to grasp the meaning of art together with how and why art can speak so powerfully to us. The impact of the Nazi regime on Kollwitz and her contemporaries leads to consideration of the totalitarian view of the purpose of art and consequently what we mean by ‘art’. Finally, the author perceives the art of Kollwitz as a life-long self-analysis and considers this as a mirror to the concept of psychoanalysis as an art. In her exploration of the arts she applies Bion's concept of ‘O’ (the thing-in-itself) and its transformations to understand and give meaning to the arts.

BINGEING, SOBRIETY, ADDICTION, TIME, POSITIONS

Every psychotherapist working in the challenging field of the addictions is familiar with patients who yo-yo between extended periods of abstinence from substances, or other compulsive and non-substance-based addictive behaviours, and who then lapse or relapse to compressed periods of excessive substance misuse, the so-called binge episode. In this paper we reverse the lens of theoretical focus somewhat, from its more traditional position within the clinical field of addiction. We suggest that periods of abstinence from substance misuse, or other compulsive behaviours, may also represent a type of binge-like behaviour which satisfies, for a time, core needs though which may also invariably be non-sustainable if the underlying psychodynamic processes underscoring such repetitive abstinence binges are not explored and translated, in work with the patient. Linkage will also be made between poles of experience that addicted and substance abusing patients evince, which are here termed black holes (Sweet, 2012) and white holes (Miller, personal communication, 2015). These proposed intra-psychic structures are, it is asserted, intimately related to the ability, or not, of the individual to bear psychological pain and distress, tolerate separation from objects at both an inter-personal and intra-psychic level and to delay gratification of instinctually grounded desires and wishes. The authors reference Hopper's (1995) previous description of both black holes and white holes in the addictions, and Glasser's (1979) conception of the black hole in relation to perversion and his description of the ‘core complex’, drawing out both similarities and differences in the viewpoints presented. Key ideas in the paper are illuminated and contextualized through the presentation of a number of illustrative clinical examples.

WINNICOTT, LANGUAGE, PSYCHOANALYSIS, METAPSYCHOLOGY

The author makes a plea for a reading of Winnicott's writings that searches for Winnicott's way of thinking besides searching for specific ideas and concepts. He addresses the question of Winnicott's language, which, the author suggests, may reveal itself at odds not so much with classical Freudian psychoanalysis, as is often purported, as with an entrenched and dogmatic attitude that reigned in many quarters of the psychoanalytic community around him. A parallel reading of his papers and of his correspondence shows that Winnicott avoided writing in a desiccated, formulaic fashion or in reverence to some leading figure in the psychoanalytic society. He rather opted for thinking his own thoughts and thinking the psychoanalytic experience anew.

Lesley Caldwell

Lesley Caldwell  

These papers were given at the IPA Congress in Boston in July 2015 in a panel organized under the auspices of the Winnicott Trust to publicize the forthcoming Collected Works of Donald Winnicott (OUP, 2016 in press). The panel was organized by Lesley Caldwell (London) and chaired by Angela Joyce, Chair of the Winnicott Trust. It gathered together international speakers from Europe and North America: Dieter Bürgin (Basel), Lesley Caldwell (London), Adrienne Harris (New York), Dominique Scarfone (Montreal). By offering a reading of Winnicott through familiar and unfamiliar themes, the panel members aimed to offer ways of thinking that would prioritize the insights of psychoanalysis in a world increasingly challenged by social and cultural transformation. In these papers reproduced in the BJP we argue for the contemporary relevance of reading Donald Winnicott for an increased understanding of the demands of psychoanalytic work today.

The panel endorsed Winnicott's lasting contribution to psychoanalytic theory and psychoanalytic practice by building upon the forthcoming Collected Works. The emphases followed by all four speakers are located in a commitment to reading and rereading, to the challenge of encountering unfamiliar or previously unpublished work alongside classic papers. They aim to develop closer knowledge of the psychoanalytic terrain Winnicott made his own through approaching them in the context of familiar and unfamiliar themes and their relevance for a psychoanalysis of the present and the future.

In extending Winnicott's writings from an over-easy familiarity that may obstruct the contemporary uses of their exceptional aspects, the papers offer an unexpected set of encounters with this consummate clinician, by seeing the work anew and making it strange. The first presentation by Dominique Scarfone, based on his introduction to volume 4 of the Collected Works, argues for the value and the rewards of reading Winnicott slowly, a passionate plea for taking Winnicott seriously, and leaving to one side any easy assumptions about his work. This is a framework that was followed by all four speakers, the basis from which each paper is to be approached.

ETHICS, INNER WORLD, INTERSUBJECTIVITY, INTRAPSYCHIC LIFE, MIRROR STAGE, PSYCHIC REALITY, PSYCHOANALYTIC THEORY, SUPEREGO

Psychoanalytic theory attributes the development of morality largely to the role of the superego, as the internalization of authority that helps the ego live within the constraints of reality. Conscience is born when the infant is able to imagine the feelings of another, to see that his actions have an impact on others, and to experience concern. This is the attainment of the depressive position in which good and bad are no longer split and kept separate from one another but coexist within the same object, just as the child can experience both love and hate towards his object. While having a conscience and doing the ‘right’ thing reflect larger group norms that develop from childhood, is there nevertheless an idea of ‘right’ and ‘wrong’ that precedes the tenets of the group? This paper proposes that our sense of morality is based on our initial perception of ourselves, as mirrored by the observing ego, and the degree to which our experience of reality is validated internally. The idea of ‘being true to oneself’ is the fundamental cornerstone of moral sensibility.

Psychoses without Symptoms and Stabilized Psychoses: Lacanian Suggestions for Treating Fuzzy Contemporary Clinical Phenomena

Federica Facchin PHD

Federica Facchin

Largo A. Gemelli 1, Milan, MI 20123, Italy. [federica.facchin@unicatt.it]

Federica Facchin   Research fellow in the Department of Psychology, Catholic University of Milan, where she is lecturer in clinical psychology of family relationships. She has been an international visiting scholar and lecturer at several universities, such as the Catholic University of Portugal in Braga. She trained as a Lacanian psychoanalyst at the Freudian Institute of Milan, where she is currently lecturer in psychopathology.
LACAN, JOUISSANCE, NEO-TRIGGERING, SUPPLETION, ORDINARY PSYCHOSIS

Multiple clinical phenomena cannot be easily classified as either neurotic or psychotic; they may be considered as ‘fuzzy’. Contemporary Lacanian perspectives may offer theoretical and clinical tools to clarify and treat these ‘fuzzy’ clinical phenomena. This article presents two clinical cases, reviews Lacan's classical teaching (1950s) and later conceptualizations (1970s) with a specific focus on foreclosure of the Name-of-the-Father, the jouissance, and notions of triggering and stabilization. The two clinical cases are discussed highlighting limitations of classical Lacanian conceptualizations and advantages of the contemporary theories focused on the notions of jouissance, suppletion and ordinary psychosis. Overall, this article aims at providing an understanding of clinical situations that are no longer ‘rare cases’, but rather require an approach that emphasizes treatment flexibility and uniqueness of the subjective devices that allow one to manage the jouissance.

The Private Life: Why We Remain in the Dark A Response to Roger Bacon

Josh Cohen

Josh Cohen

[j.cohen@gold.ac.uk]

Josh Cohen  

It is gratifying to see The Private Life provide occasion for such an expansive, intelligent and theoretically cosmopolitan discussion of the fundamental but too often neglected question of psychoanalytic aims (BJP 31(4), November 2015). I find much to enjoy and learn from in Roger Bacon's review essay, above all in his subtle adumbration and development of Guyomard's notion of a ‘third space’, in which privacy is understood as a ‘capacity’ born from the paradoxical intimacy of the analytic relation. Whether this sense of privacy is as far from my own as the review suggests is another question, to which I'll duly return.

After two careful readings, I'm left wondering why the attentive intimacy which models Bacon's conception of the analytic relation doesn't carry over to his reading of the book. The roughly one third of the review that discusses The Private Life directly does so by way of a summary and largely inaccurate reduction of its arguments to a series of propositional claims that can then be shown up for their ‘confusions and contradictions’. This in turn serves as the springboard for the exposition of a corrective (and very suggestive) conception of analytic privacy in supposed opposition to mine.

By boiling its content down to a series of discrete propositions with which to agree or disagree, the review sets up an adversarial relation to the book, closing down the very dialogue it might have opened up. There is very little attention to the paradoxes and ambiguities which shape both its arguments and its winding, associative style. In a review of 6000 words, only two passages are directly referenced, one an anecdote, the other its two concluding paragraphs, quoted in full as though their meaning were self-evident and required no contextualization or gloss beyond their summarily dismissive and question-begging description as ‘deeply Romantic’.

Why should Bacon set up his model of privacy in such stark contrast to mine, as though there were no points of contact or affinities between them? It is a stance resulting in a series of misrepresentations of the book so basic I feel bound to counter them, at the risk of a tone of wounded narcissistic protest that perpetuates the oppositional mood of the review itself.

Richard Carvalho

Richard Carvalho

[rrncarvalho@btinternet.com]

Richard Carvalho   Fellow of the Royal College of Psychiatrists, a member of the Tavistock Society of Psychotherapists, a training and supervising analyst of the Society of Analytical Psychology as well as for other bodies. He was consultant psychotherapist at St Mary's Hospital in Paddington, London for 16 years.
ASSESSMENT, ABILITY TO ENGAGE, MOTIVATION, TREATMENT CHOICES, RECORDS, VIGNETTES

The author offers personal rather than scholarly reflections on the sometimes difficult process of assessment. He discusses aims of assessment which include risk assessment, and an assessment of the prospective patient's ability to engage in the therapeutic process as indicated by their engagement with the assessor's interpretive remarks, albeit oppositionally or defensively, and whether consciously or unconsciously. Implicit or explicit in this engagement will be the issue of the patient's habitual ways of relating, the transference. Consideration is also given to how we can evaluate the nature of the patient's motivation, not only with regard to insight and change, but also to dependency and malignancy. The issue of treatment choices is discussed, along with the desirability of any management decisions being offered as interpretations. The author also addresses the issue of note and record writing in the light of the scope this gives for countertransference enactment, as well as the issue of what records are kept for what purposes and of how and when these are communicated to GPs. Vignettes illustrate some of the difficulties and pitfalls of the process.

Researching Psychodynamic Psychotherapy for Psychosis: Are We Ready Yet?

Rachel Waddingham

Rachel Waddingham

[rachel@behindthelabel.co.uk, www.behindthelabel.co.uk]

Rachel Waddingham   Trainer and consultant specializing in developing respectful approaches to supporting those who struggle with voices, visions, overwhelming beliefs and post-traumatic reactions. She managed the London Hearing Voices Project from 2007 to 2015, where she launched an innovative project developing a sustainable network of Hearing Voices Groups in London's prisons and in forensic hospitals as well as establishing Voice Collective to creatively support children and young people who hear voices, and their families. She is a media spokesperson, a trustee of the National Hearing Voices Network and a co-opted board member of Intervoice. She hears voices, sees visions and - during her 20s - spent years in hospital diagnosed with schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder. She is Vice Chair of ISPS UK and an Executive Committee member of the International Society for Psychological and Social Approaches to Psychosis.

I write this as a person who has experience of that thing we call psychosis, an experience that has run through a range of diagnoses (from schizophrenia to dissociative identity disorder). I was asked to speak about two things for the ISPS UK conference ‘Researching Psychodynamic Psychotherapy for Psychosis’1: (1) Why is it important for people who experience ‘psychosis’ to have access to psychodynamic psychotherapy? (2) What should be researched in this area? These two questions are more complex than they may seem on first reading.

Why is it Important for People Who Experience ‘Psychosis’ to Have Access to Psychodynamic Psychotherapy?

This answer is easy - it's about choice. There are multiple pathways to ‘recovery’ for those in distress. If someone wants to choose the psychodynamic route, we should do all we can to make this available to them. However, I also think that people have the right to choose a whole range of pathways - including cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), medication, art therapy, spiritual release and tai chi. In a world where our evidence for interventions is flawed, surely we each have the right to choose the range of options we find most helpful to manage our mental wellbeing?

But, do I think that we should encourage people to try psychodynamic psychotherapy as a treatment option? Should the NHS invest more in it? My answer to this is that, in all honesty, I don't know. That is why we need research.

My own feelings about this modality are complex. On the one hand, I recognize the value in an approach that can, when done well, provide people with the precious opportunity to be heard. I welcome therapeutic relationships that help create the space for people to explore and reflect on powerful experiences, finding meaning in what people often dismiss as incoherent or ‘mad’. This appreciation of personal meaning is an oasis in a more positivist culture where we are all too often seduced by the perceived concrete certainty of biology and time-limited manualized therapies (e.g. CBT).

Clinical Commentary 36

Mark Budden and Ann Home

Ann Home

[markbudden@talktalk.net]

[annhorne44@gmail.com]

Ann Home   Fellow of the British Psychoanalytic Foundation, which she represents on the Editorial Board of the BJP.

The Clinical Commentaries were a regular feature in the British Journal of Psychotherapy from the first issue in 1984 to the 35th commentary in 2007. They offered clinicians an opportunity to think carefully about a detailed piece of clinical work, formulate their own thoughts about it, and then read the responses of the commentators. This opportunity to ‘play’ with clinical material and reflect on the different responses and approaches of the commentators was often not only an enlivening and enjoyable reading experience in itself, but also helped readers to clarify their own ideas in relation to those of the commentators. Ann Scott, the editor of the BJP, has been keen to revive and develop the clinical commentaries and we are delighted to be introducing the first of what we hope will become a regular bi-annual feature of the BJP.

We are very grateful to the therapist who has offered the clinical material which follows. It requires a particular quality of generosity to offer clinical material in this context, as well as a relatively low level of paranoid anxiety. We hope that you will enjoy reading the material and will be able to take a moment to formulate your own responses to it, before reading the responses of the commentators.

Those offering clinical material are invited to present material from one session, or from one session with brief reference to material from the previous or subsequent session, and to give enough of the context in which the work takes place, of the patient's history, and of the stage in the therapy when the clinical material occurs, to orientate the reader. We also ask to hear something about the questions, dilemmas or difficulties that the work presents to the therapist at the time the clinical exchanges take place.

It is of the essence of these commentaries that the clinical material is offered anonymously, and so there are none of the benefits of recognition and reputation as a compensation for the considerable work put into the writing. It really is a generous offering to the psychoanalytic community. However, we hope that this anonymity may allow the therapist to write with some greater freedom than when writing under their own name.

A Chance to Show His Mettle: War, Creativity and Reparation in the Work of Wilfred Bion

Caroline Ballinger

Caroline Ballinger

[crballinger@hotmail.co.uk]

Caroline Ballinger   Student on the MA in Psychoanalytic Studies at Birkbeck, University of London, for which she initially wrote this paper. She is a trainee at The Site for Contemporary Psychoanalysis and an honorary psychotherapist at The Gordon Hospital.
BION, TRAUMA, KLEIN, REPARATION, CREATIVITY

This paper looks in detail at Wilfred Bion's war writings, specifically at his preoccupation with issues of morale and leadership, and at the intense feelings of isolation and disillusionment that accompany his bleakest moments. This reading of the war writings demonstrates that Bion found resources that enabled him not only to survive this harrowing time but also to work creatively to improve the lives of his fellow soldiers, and it is suggested that Melanie Klein's concept of unconscious reparation may be helpful in considering Bion's life and work during this period. An impulse to repair may also be discerned in Bion's first published paper, ‘The “war of nerves” …’ (1940), as well as in his work in 1942 for the War Office Selection Board where, with the support of gifted army leaders, Bion was able to draw on his traumatic wartime experiences in order to make influential contributions to the reform of the British Army.

Lacan on Madness: Madness, Yes You Can't edited by Patricia Gherovici and Manya Steinkoler. Published by Routledge, London and New York, 2015; 274 pp; £29.99 (paperback)

Anne Worthington

Anne Worthington

a.worthington@mdx.ac.uk

Anne Worthington  

Not only can man's being not be understood without madness, but it would not be man's being if it did not bear madness within itself as the limit of his freedom … Not just anyone can go mad. (Lacan, 1946, p. 144)

The collection of papers edited by Gherovici and Steinkoler can be read as something of a commentary on this statement from Lacan. The idea that madness holds some clue to solving the mystery of our very being is appealing. We all imagine that we have experienced something of madness - when we are in love, in our dreams, when struck by grief. Surely madness leads to some understanding? Some essential truth of being human? Some knowledge? So too does the association between madness and freedom appeal. Surely only the crazy woman, the mad artist, the screaming queen, the fanatical revolutionary knows the exit from the box of convention/oppression? Nevertheless both the figure of the mad man and the feeling that we're going crazy are terrifying. Perhaps then, the idea that ‘not just anyone can go mad’ engenders both some disappointment and some relief.

Readers less familiar with the Lacanian tradition may be surprised by the essays in this volume which challenge the idea that madness is an illness, and thus the hierarchy of suffering in which psychosis is somehow so much ‘worse’ than neurosis and therefore inaccessible to clinical work, or that it is something to be avoided as its manifestations are meaningless. On the other hand, the mad man or woman is deemed to be so sick, so disordered that he must be set right by the clinician who has the better grip on reality and who knows how to be healthy.
